accepted.question_text: Determine, before carrying out a full reduction calculation, which partial differential equations have symmetry reductions that cannot be obtained by the classical Lie group method. The classical Lie group method is the standard infinitesimal-transformation approach to symmetry reductions; the problem asks for an a priori criterion distinguishing equations for which generalized methods such as nonclassical or direct methods are genuinely needed.
accepted.context_brief: limits of the classical Lie group method

evidence.quote: Open Question 2.1. How does one determine a priori which partial diﬀerential equations possess symmetry reductions that are not obtainable using the classical Lie group approach?

accepted.question_text: Develop algorithms for solving the overdetermined systems of equations that arise when applying symmetry methods to partial differential equations with a high degree of symmetry.

evidence.quote: Open Question 2.2. To develop algorithms to solve overdetermined systems associated with partial diﬀerential equations which have a high degree of symmetry.

accepted.question_text: Find a general procedure for applying symmetry methods to boundary value problems, rather than only applying the standard classical requirement that both the differential equation and all boundary conditions be invariant under the same one-parameter Lie group.
accepted.context_brief: symmetry methods for boundary value problems

evidence.quote: Open Question 2.3. Is there a general procedure, for applying symmetry methods to boundary value problems?
The standard procedure for applying the classical method (cf. [5]) to the boundary value problem (2.12-2.14) is to require that both equation and boundary conditions are invariant

accepted.question_text: Clarify how the different approaches to symmetry reductions of differential-difference equations and difference equations are related to one another, and, if possible, formulate a single standard definition of a symmetry for such equations.

evidence.quote: Open Question 2.4. To clarify the relationship of these approaches (if possible) to each other, and to produce a single standard deﬁnition of a symmetry of diﬀerential-diﬀerence (and diﬀerence) equations.

accepted.question_text: Develop the study of nonclassical symmetry reductions for differential-difference equations and difference equations.

evidence.quote: Open Question 2.5. The study of nonclassical symmetry reductions of diﬀerential-diﬀerence and diﬀerence equations.

accepted.question_text: For a nonlocal differential equation that can be rewritten in several analytic scalar or system representations, determine in advance which representation is most suitable for symmetry calculations.
accepted.context_brief: representing nonlocal equations for symmetry calculations

evidence.quote: Open Question 2.6. How does one determine a priori the most suitable representation, from the point of view of symmetry calculations, of a nonlocal equation such as (2.19)?

accepted.question_text: Determine whether nonclassical generalized symmetries exist, and, if they do exist, characterize the kinds of solutions they generate.

evidence.quote: Open Question 2.7. Do nonclassical, generalized symmetries exist and if so what kind of solutions do they generate?

accepted.question_text: Design and further develop numerical algorithms for ordinary differential equations and especially partial differential equations that inherit symmetries of the differential equations, including nonclassical symmetries.

evidence.quote: Open Question 2.8. The design and further development of numerical algorithms for ordinary and, in particular, partial diﬀerential equations which inherit symmetries of the diﬀerential equations including nonclassical symmetries.

accepted.question_text: Find an a priori way to decide which differential constraints are useful for finding special solutions of differential equations, and which ansatz choices will lead to computable solutions.
accepted.context_brief: choosing useful differential constraints and ansatze

evidence.quote: Open Question 2.9. How does one determine a priori which diﬀerential constraints are useful and which ansätze will yield computable solutions?
